name: Unibrow trimming / bridge shaping

lead: A unibrow, or synophrys, is hair connecting the eyebrows over the bridge of the nose. Removing or shaping it makes the brows look like two separate arcs and gives a tidier, more open upper face, visible immediately.

It is a common, usually harmless polygenic trait. Cultural views differ: connected brows are admired in some historical and modern settings and not in many Western ones. No studies have tested how bridge shaping changes perceived attractiveness.

paras: People pluck, wax, thread, shave or trim the glabella hair. Plucking and waxing pull from the root and it regrows over weeks, while laser and electrolysis target the follicle for longer-lasting reduction.
Grooming can cause temporary redness, pain or ingrown hairs. Rarely, synophrys is one feature of a genetic syndrome, which is a medical rather than cosmetic matter.

chain: Brows read as two clean arcs
angle.text: Users pluck, wax, thread or shave the bridge between the brows so they read as two clean arcs and the area above the nose looks tidy. The result is visible immediately and reversible, and whether a unibrow counts as a flaw varies by culture.

lead: A unibrow, medically called synophrys, is hair that joins the two eyebrows across the glabella, the smooth area above the bridge of the nose. Unibrow trimming or bridge shaping is the grooming practice of removing or thinning that hair, by plucking, waxing, threading, shaving, or in some cases longer-lasting hair removal, so that the brows read as two separate arches, or of deliberately keeping and shaping the bridge [1][2][3].

People do it to give the eye area a cleaner frame. Removing the bridge hair is among the cheapest, quickest and most reversible changes available to the brow outline, and before-and-after photos of it are shared in appearance forums [4]. In a number of cultures the opposite aim holds: joined brows are admired and sometimes drawn in with makeup [3].

Synophrys is a common, usually harmless trait. A 2021 review in Clinics in Dermatology describes it as usually a normal variation, and in rare cases a skin marker for genetic disorders, most often Cornelia de Lange syndrome [2][5]. A genome-wide study of 26,806 Chinese participants linked unibrow to the FARSB gene region [5].
infobox: Synophrys; from Greek words meaning together and eyebrow [2]
Tweezing, waxing, threading, shaving, trimming; laser or electrolysis for longer-lasting removal [4][12][11]
Associated with the PAX3 gene region in Wikipedia; a 2022 GWAS reported a locus at FARSB [3][5]
About 11.9 percent of the population studied [3]
Admired in some societies, often removed in much of Europe and the Americas [2][3]

paras: A unibrow forms when terminal hair grows across the glabella, linking the medial ends of the two brows. The hair is usually the same colour and thickness as the brows, so the two appear to form one continuous line [2][3]. Density ranges from a faint line to a fully joined band [1].

Eyebrows keep sweat and debris away from the eyes and are thought to have developed in humans largely as a means of communication, which is part of why their shape draws attention [4]. Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia, reports that androgens such as testosterone and dihydrotestosterone influence terminal hair density in facial regions including the glabella; this has not been independently verified here [1].

Wikipedia cites a study that found synophrys in 11.87 percent of the Omani population [3]. Wikipedia describes the unibrow as a genetic trait associated with the PAX3 gene [3]. A 2022 genome-wide association study of 26,806 Chinese participants examined five facial traits, including unibrow, and reported one novel locus for unibrow at FARSB [6][5].

Synophrys also appears in case reports and reviews of rare genetic conditions, where it is one of several facial features rather than a stand-alone sign. These include Cornelia de Lange syndrome, Snijders Blok-Campeau syndrome and 1p36 deletion syndrome [7][2][8]. Wikipedia notes that rare PAX3 mutations cause Waardenburg syndrome type 1, in which about 85 percent of patients have a unibrow [3].

Other published reports include transient fetal hypertrichosis and a case of bilateral milia en plaque of the eyelids with long eyelashes and unibrow [9][10]. The dermatology review frames these as reasons clinicians pay attention to the sign, while stating that in most people it is simply a variation [2].

Wikipedia describes tweezing as the most common brow-grooming method, with waxing growing in popularity and threading and small scissors also used; it notes removal can hurt at first and that the discomfort often fades over time [4]. Threading rolls a doubled thread over hair to lift short rows at once; it originated in the Middle East and South Asia and reached Western salons in the 1980s, when an Iranian beautician reportedly introduced it in Germany [11]. Practitioners cite precise control when shaping brows and a gentler effect on skin than waxing [11].
Shaving and trimming with small scissors or a brow trimmer are the quickest options.

Laser hair removal targets melanin in the follicle. Wikipedia reports that many people need at least eight sessions spaced about three to eight weeks apart, that results are best on dark, coarse hair, and that under the FDA definition it achieves permanent hair reduction rather than guaranteed total removal; the technique became commercially available in 1995 to 1996 [12]. Reported risks include redness, swelling, burns, skin discoloration and infection [12]. Electrolysis is another method discussed for permanent removal.

Bridge shaping means choosing where each brow begins and how much space sits between them. Brow products such as gels, powders and pencils add fullness, tinting darkens brows, and cosmetic tattooing or microblading implants pigment to mimic hair; brow transplants move follicles from the scalp [4]. Some people keep a faint bridge, and in cultures that favour joined brows, makeup is used to create or deepen it [3].

The word monobrow first appeared in print in 1968, and the adjective monobrowed followed in 1973 in Martin Amis's novel The Rachel Papers; the first known use of unibrow dates to 1981 [3]. Brow fashion has varied widely: Japanese women and men from the 8th century practised hikimayu, shaving or plucking the brows and painting them higher, and thin plucked brows were fashionable in the 1920s and 1930s [4].

Wikipedia reports that unibrows are a sign of beauty among Baluchi Omanis, whose women sometimes draw a line to join their brows, and that some Tajik women use a local herb called usma or kohl to simulate one; in the Americas and Europe the trait is largely seen as undesirable and the hair is commonly plucked, shaved or waxed [3]. Frida Kahlo, who often depicted her unibrow in self-portraits, is cited as a prominent exception, along with the model Sophia Hadjipanteli and the actor Omar Ayuso [3]. The NBA player Anthony Davis is known for his unibrow and trademarked it, and footballer Marouane Fellaini and the YouTuber ElectroBOOM are also associated with the look [3].

Grokipedia adds that joined brows were admired in ancient Greece and Rome and in Persian poetry [1]. A 2021 review states that many cultures have historically valued synophrys as attractive while modern Western culture often sees it as unappealing [2][5].

On looksmax.org, users post before-and-after photos of shaved unibrows and ask for ratings of the brows and eye area, with replies ranging from mixed to mildly positive. Brow grooming is generally treated as a low-cost, reversible adjustment within wider discussion of the eyes, brow ridge and canthal features.

Plucking, waxing and threading can cause temporary redness, pain, irritation and ingrown hairs, and laser hair removal has the risks listed above [4][12][11]. Wikipedia advises, in its Unibrow article, that hair in the area be removed carefully without causing inflammation and with a disinfectant or antiseptic [3]. Where synophrys appears with other facial or developmental features, clinicians treat it as a prompt for medical assessment rather than a cosmetic matter [7][2].

No studies found on the effect of unibrow trimming on appearance or attractiveness. Related research concerns genetics and syndromes, such as the GWAS of aesthetic facial traits in a Chinese population, the Omani prevalence study cited by Wikipedia, and case series on associated conditions [6][7][3][5].

lore.intro: Unibrow removal is discussed on forums as an easy, reversible step for the eye area, with before-and-after photo threads asking for ratings.
